chief_complaint: irregular, asymmetric, ulcerated, and bleeding pigmented skin lesion on the back
hpi_details: 50M presenting with a new, rapidly growing, asymmetric pigmented lesion on the posterior trunk with irregular borders, color variegation, and recent ulceration and bleeding, clinically concerning for melanoma.
ideas: He thinks the dark spot is an irritated mole or a blood blister that ruptured from friction against his heavy work backpack straps.
concerns: He is worried that the dark spot is a malignant skin cancer that has already begun spreading through his bloodstream because it started bleeding.
expectations: He hopes to have the lesion cut out or biopsied today to find out immediately whether it is dangerous.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Malignant Melanoma is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes full-thickness excisional biopsy for histologic diagnosis before determining excision margins or sentinel node eligibility, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: irregular, asymmetric, ulcerated, and bleeding pigmented skin lesion on the back

Key HPI features: 50M presenting with a new, rapidly growing, asymmetric pigmented lesion on the posterior trunk with irregular borders, color variegation, and recent ulceration and bleeding, clinically concerning for melanoma.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals normal. Posterior trunk lesion approximately 1.8 cm in diameter, asymmetric with irregular, notched borders and variegated brown-black-red coloration; surface ulcerated with crusting and bleeding on contact. No palpable regional (axillary) lymphadenopathy. Full skin exam performed to screen for additional atypical or satellite lesions.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Malignant Melanoma.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dysplastic nevus without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breslow depth predictors (ulceration, rapid vertical growth).
management_principles: Diagnose with a full-thickness excisional biopsy (narrow 1-3mm margins), not a shave or punch biopsy, to accurately assess Breslow depth, ulceration, and mitotic rate
Definitive wide local excision margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy eligibility are determined by the pathologic Breslow depth once confirmed, not before
Refer to a multidisciplinary melanoma team for staging (imaging, LDH as indicated) and surgical planning after histologic confirmation
Perform a full skin exam and screen regional lymph nodes for additional lesions or nodal spread at every visit.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 50M presenting with a new, rapidly growing, asymmetric pigmented lesion on the posterior trunk with irregular borders, color variegation, and recent ulceration and bleeding, clinically concerning for melanoma.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals normal. Posterior trunk lesion approximately 1.8 cm in diameter, asymmetric with irregular, notched borders and variegated brown-black-red coloration; surface ulcerated with crusting and bleeding on contact. No palpable regional lymphadenopathy. Full skin exam performed.
reference_soap.assessment: Pigmented lesion with multiple ABCDE features and ulceration/bleeding, highly concerning for melanoma; histologic diagnosis including Breslow depth requires excisional biopsy.
reference_soap.plan: Obtain a full-thickness excisional biopsy with narrow margins for histologic diagnosis, Breslow thickness, ulceration status, and mitotic rate. Once melanoma is confirmed, the pathologic Breslow depth determines definitive wide local excision margins and whether sentinel lymph node biopsy is indicated. Refer to a multidisciplinary melanoma team for staging workup and definitive surgical planning.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of Melanoma Wide Local Excision Sentinel Lymph Node
Formulate prioritized differential diagnosis for irregular, asymmetric pigmented skin lesion measuring 2.4 mm Breslow depth on back
Select the appropriate biopsy technique (full-thickness excisional biopsy) and staging studies for a suspected melanoma
Implement evidence-based acute and long-term management strategies

teaching.one_liner: Aggressive skin malignancy arising from melanocytes, requiring urgent excisional biopsy.
red_flags: Breslow depth predictors (ulceration, rapid vertical growth)

must_ask.say: Is the mole asymmetrical with irregular, notched, or blurred borders?
Does the mole contain multiple different colors like black, brown, red, or blue?
Has the spot grown larger than 6 millimeters or changed size, shape, or height recently?
Does the spot itch, bleed spontaneously, or form a crust?
Do you have a history of severe blistering sunburns or tanning bed use?

history.answer: I noticed a dark spot on my back that has been growing quickly over the past few months, and lately it started bleeding and forming crusts.
My wife first noticed it about four months ago, and it has been rapidly changing and growing ever since.
It is right in the center of my upper back, in a spot that is difficult for me to see clearly on my own.
It started out as a tiny speck, but it grew rapidly over four months to the size of a coin.
It is just that single spot on my back; I have not found any other new or unusual moles anywhere else.

It does not hurt when left alone, but it stings and feels sore when my clothes rub against it or when pressed.

It has multiple colors mixed together, including dark brown, jet black, and some reddish patches.
Over the last two weeks it started bleeding easily whenever my shirt grazes it, and it forms a crust that never truly heals.
Yes, it bleeds with minimal friction, and it has felt persistently itchy and irritated for the past couple of weeks.
No, there is no spreading redness around it, no sensation of feverish heat, and no yellow pus or bad smell.

No, it has only grown larger steadily and has never shrunk, faded, or fluctuated in size.

No, I have not had any fever, night sweats, unplanned weight loss, or swollen lumps in my armpits or neck.
I spend lots of time outdoors running and hiking, and I had several severe blistering sunburns on my shoulders and back when I was younger.
I used indoor tanning beds a couple of times a month during my college years, though I have not used one since.
I have never had skin cancer before, and as far as I know, no one in my family has ever been diagnosed with melanoma or other skin cancers.
No, I have not tried to squeeze it, scratch it off, or apply any over-the-counter ointments; I came straight to the doctor.

I'm hoping you can remove it or take a biopsy today so I can know for sure what I'm dealing with.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.6°C, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert, well-nourished middle-aged male sitting comfortably in no acute distress.

An asymmetric pigmented plaque measuring 1.8 cm in diameter on the mid-upper back with irregular, notched borders, variegated brown, black, and red coloration, and central ulceration with crusting that bleeds on contact; full-body skin examination reveals no other atypical, dysplastic, or satellite pigmented lesions.
No palpable lymphadenopathy or masses in either axilla; bilateral axillary vaults are soft and nontender.
No palpable cervical, supraclavicular, or occipital lymph nodes detected bilaterally.
